conventions: signal/ancilla register is high-order, system register is low-order
source_semantics.question: A block-encoding unitary represents an operator that acts on the 2^n states of an n-qubit system register, using a auxiliary qubits. (a) What is the dimension of the square matrix representing the full unitary, and why? (b) The full index is a flattened combination of a signal/ancilla register and the system register; state which register is treated as the high-order (most significant) part of the index and which as the low-order part. (c) If one instead keeps the two registers explicit as an ordered pair (signal, system) and reads off the sub-matrix for one fixed value of the signal register, how does that sub-matrix relate to the sub-matrix obtained by projecting the single flattened unitary onto the same signal branch?
source_semantics.reference_answer: (a) The full unitary is a 2^(n+a) by 2^(n+a) matrix. The combined register has n + a qubits (n system qubits plus a auxiliary qubits), and a register of n+a qubits has 2^(n+a) basis states, so the unitary acting on all of them is a square matrix of that size. (b) The signal/ancilla register is the high-order (most significant) part of the flattened index and the system register is the low-order part; equivalently the flat index is signalIndex times (system dimension) plus systemIndex. (c) They are the same matrix. Taking the explicit product-register view of the flat unitary and then extracting the block for one fixed signal value yields exactly the same entries, position by position, as projecting the single flattened unitary onto that signal branch; the two descriptions are definitionally identical, so reasoning done in either view transfers to the other without any change of entries.

source_semantics.question: In a finite complex matrix backend, acting with an operator on a computational-basis state (a vector with a single 1 at one position and 0 elsewhere) returns the corresponding column of the operator. Using only this fact and the linearity of matrix-vector multiplication, prove that acting with an operator A on the two-term superposition a*|left> + b*|right>, where |left> and |right> are two basis states, gives a*(column left of A) + b*(column right of A), and that the amplitude read at output row k equals a*A[k,left] + b*A[k,right]. Explain why this means a block-encoding or state-preparation witness never needs to reconstruct the whole matrix-vector product: only two named columns, or two named entries, are ever required.
source_semantics.reference_answer: Matrix-vector multiplication is linear in the vector argument: for scalars a, b and vectors u, w we have A(a*u + b*w) = a*(A u) + b*(A w), and A(c*u) = c*(A u). Apply this with u = |left> and w = |right>. By the basis-column fact, A|left> is exactly the 'left' column of A and A|right> is exactly the 'right' column of A. Therefore A(a*|left> + b*|right>) = a*(A|left>) + b*(A|right>) = a*(column left of A) + b*(column right of A). Reading the k-th coordinate of both sides and using that the k-th coordinate of the 'j' column of A is the entry A[k,j], the output amplitude at row k is a*A[k,left] + b*A[k,right]. Consequently, to certify what an operator does to any two-term superposition it suffices to inspect the two named columns (vector form) or, for a single output amplitude, just the two named matrix entries (scalar form). No sum over all basis states or full reconstruction of the matrix-vector product is needed; the sparsity of the input collapses the computation to exactly the terms whose input amplitude is nonzero. This is why finite preparation and block-encoding witnesses are stated and checked column-wise or entry-wise rather than by rebuilding a dense product.

source_semantics.question: A reversible gate flips a target bit exactly when two control bits are both1. Assume each control wire is distinct from the target, but allow the two control wires to coincide. Prove the gate is its own inverse and explain what it reduces to when the controls coincide.
source_semantics.reference_answer: If the control predicate is false, the gate leaves the whole bit string unchanged, so a second application also does nothing. If true, it flips only the target; each control remains1 because neither control is the target. Thus the predicate remains true for the second application, which flips the target back. All other bits stay fixed, proving involution. If the two controls coincide, the condition c=1 and c=1 is just c=1, so the action reduces to one controlled bit flip. Pairwise-distinct controls are required by some instruction encodings but not by this involution argument; control-target distinctness is the load-bearing condition.

source_semantics.question: On a two-bit string(c,t), consider the update that flips c itself when c=t=1 and otherwise does nothing. Does the familiar self-inverse proof for a two-control target flip remain valid when one control is also the target? Give a concrete collision and explain the lost hypothesis.
source_semantics.reference_answer: No. The input(1,1) is sent to(0,1), while(0,1) already fails the activation predicate and is left at(0,1). Two distinct inputs therefore collide, so this map is not injective and cannot be reversible or unitary on basis states. Applying it twice to(1,1) does not return the original state: after the first flip the control predicate became false. The usual involution proof uses that flipping the target preserves all control bits, which fails exactly when a control coincides with the target. This is a mathematical counterexample, not a compiler rejection.
